Chapter 9: When Anxiety Persists—Knowing When to Seek Extra Support
Sometimes, even with our best efforts and all the self-help strategies in the world, social anxiety can just hang on. If you’ve been working hard but that anxiety still feels stubborn or overwhelming, you’re not alone.
Here’s something to remember: reaching out for extra support isn’t a sign of failure—it’s actually a powerful act of self-care. You’re giving yourself the chance to discover new tools, fresh perspectives, and a little extra encouragement when you need it most.
Therapy, especially cognitive-behavioral therapy—or CBT as it’s often called—has been shown to be really effective for social anxiety. A good therapist can help you spot those unhelpful patterns, guide you through exposure exercises in a safe way, and keep you accountable as you make progress.
There’s also group therapy, which can be surprisingly comforting. Imagine being in a space where you can practice social skills and realize you aren’t the only one with these struggles. It’s a chance to connect, learn, and support each other.
In some situations, medication might be worth considering—especially if your anxiety is really severe or gets in the way of your daily life. This is a personal choice, and it’s best to talk it through with a healthcare provider you trust.
The important thing is this: reaching out takes courage. It shows that you value your own well-being and that you’re willing to invest in your growth. Even when you work with a professional, the key principles still apply—self-compassion, gradual exposure, and staying true to yourself.
So, how do you know when it might be time to seek extra support? Here are a few signs to look out for:
First, you might notice persistent, intense anxiety—when fear keeps getting in the way of work, relationships, or just everyday things.
Second, maybe you find yourself avoiding most social situations, to the point where it’s hard to do the things that matter to you.
Third, if you’re feeling hopeless or down for long stretches, or you’ve lost interest in things you used to enjoy, that’s a good reason to reach out.
And finally, if you’re just hungry for faster progress, or self-help strategies aren’t feeling like enough, it might be time for a little extra guidance.
Let me share something inspiring—real people, just like you, have found that getting help can be transformative. With the right support, changes that once seemed out of reach suddenly become possible.
Remember, you deserve support. And sometimes, the bravest thing you can do is simply ask for it.
